title: Effort
hookLine: the fifth perfection, taught with a lute string
tomorrow: why keep swimming when there's no shore in sight?

cards: Crank a guitar string past its note and it whines sharp, then snaps. Loosen it and it flaps, a dull thud, no note at all. Anyone who has tuned an instrument knows both sounds.
A monk named Sona knew them too. Before he became a monk, the story goes, he played the lute.
Now he's pushing so hard at walking meditation that, the text says, his feet bleed, and he's starting to think about giving it all up.

teach.b: The Buddha comes to him with a question about music. When your lute's strings were too tight, did it play well? No.
Too loose? No. Neither too tight nor too loose, tuned to an even pitch?
Then, yes. Just so, the Buddha says: energy pushed too hard turns into restlessness, and energy too slack turns into laziness. Find the even pitch.

That's the fifth perfection, viriya: effort, energy, the get-up-and-go of the path. A popular picture says Buddhism is about not trying, floating along, letting things be. The texts don't sound like that.
The Dhammapada calls earnestness the path to the deathless.
And the Buddha names four right efforts: keep unwholesome states from arising, let go of the ones that have arisen, bring up wholesome ones, and keep the wholesome ones going. That's energy for good.
But the Sona story adds a musician's ear. Effort isn't the most you can do.

teach.h: THE AMOUNT THAT MAKES A NOTE.
teach.b: It's the amount that makes a clear note.
The story says Sona took the advice, tuned his effort, and became an arahant, fully awakened. Same monk, same feet, different tension.

how: Theravada teachers often use Sona's lute simile when students strain or slacken in meditation; viriya is counted among the ten perfections and among the spiritual faculties a practitioner balances.

o: steady energy put toward the good
a calm that comes from doing nothing
forcing yourself on until it hurts

games.q: tuning the effort — tap the pairs.

s: Buddhism teaches you to stop trying and just float
effort is a perfection, and the Buddha names four right efforts.
the Buddha used a lute to teach about effort
too tight is restless, too loose is lazy; tune it evenly.
on the path, more effort is always better
Sona pushed until his feet bled; the Buddha told him to find the even pitch.

games.q: a friend training for her first half-marathon runs hard every single day, and now her knee hurts. she says easing off means she's lazy. what would the Buddha's lute question say?
o: tune it: steady training she can keep, not the most she can do.
push through; real effort means doing the most you can.
stop running for now; effort only leads to restlessness.
games.why: too tight, the string snaps; too loose, no note. the Buddha told Sona to find the even pitch, and the story says Sona went on to awaken.

practice: Make two fists and squeeze as hard as you can for a few breaths: notice the shake and the heat. Then let your hands go completely limp.
Now find the middle, hands closed just enough to hold an egg without cracking it, and rest there for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Viriya: effort, energy for the good, the fifth perfection. Tuned like a string, not cranked.

orig.note: Pali: energy, effort for the good; the fifth of the ten perfections.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: energy for good, at the pitch that makes a clear note, not the loudest one. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: AN 6.55, Sona Sutta (the lute: too tight, too slack, evenly tuned; evenness of energy)
Dhammapada 21 (earnestness the path to the deathless)
